strengths: The supervised-SAE formulation is a useful and reasonably original extension of SAE-based concept steering. Explicitly associating labeled prompt concepts with selected latents is simple, interpretable, and practically motivated.

The main UnlearnCanvas result is strong: SAEMNESIA reports 94.65 UA, 91.39 IRA, and 88.48 CRA, improving the average from SAeUron's 82.29 to 91.51. Four-seed standard deviations are provided for these principal metrics.

The evaluation covers several relevant dimensions beyond single-concept accuracy, including retention, FID, sequential removal, multiplier sensitivity, adversarial prompting, and I2P nudity suppression. The sequential experiment is particularly promising, with 92.4% UA after nine removals versus 64% for SAeUron.

The paper is generally well organized and visually clear. Ablations compare fine-tuning and from-scratch training, alternative assignment losses, decorrelation, pre/post-TopK supervision, and uniform multipliers.
The inference intervention is lightweight and leaves the base diffusion-model weights unchanged, which can be useful when reversible or deployment-specific suppression is desired.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central claim of enforcing a one-to-one concept-latent mapping is not established by the objective. The mapping Phi independently assigns each concept its highest-scoring latent and is not constrained to be injective, while the concept-assignment loss rewards activation on positive examples but contains no explicit negative term preventing that latent from responding to other concepts. Cross-group decorrelation and L1 sparsity do not guarantee one-to-one mappings, especially within a group.

The evidence for eliminating feature splitting is insufficient. A dominant score peak and good single-feature k-NN accuracy show that one latent is predictive, not that the same concept is absent from other latents. Only a few per-concept histograms are shown, with no aggregate concentration metric across all concepts. Moreover, the selected main model has 10 Cats-Dogs overlapping timesteps in Table 8, exactly the same as SAeUron, which conflicts with the claimed systematic disentanglement.

The method applies prompt-level object and style labels to every spatial activation patch, including background and patches that may not contain the labeled object. The consequences of this noisy supervision are neither analyzed nor controlled, and the paper does not compare against simpler supervised probes or steering directions that could test whether an SAE is necessary.

The empirical scope is narrow relative to the claims of architecture agnosticism and a new standard for concept erasure: experiments use only SD v1.x, principally one SD v1.5 cross-attention block, one benchmark, and 20 object concepts. There is no evaluation on newer architectures, unseen concepts, paraphrased or compositional prompts, or transfer beyond the concepts explicitly included during supervised training.

The reported 96.67% computational-cost reduction counts hyperparameter-grid evaluations (210 versus 7), not measured runtime, memory, or end-to-end cost, and excludes supervised SAE fine-tuning and data/activation collection. Calling this a reduction in computational cost is therefore overstated.

Several results qualify the broad claims. Under UnlearnDiffAtk, UA still falls from 73.30% to 28.30%, so most attacked prompts evade suppression. For nudity, the advertised single-latent method is worse than SAeUron (47 versus 18 detections); the best result of 9 uses two latents, directly contradicting the universal single-latent narrative. The reason given—two nudity prompts—does not demonstrate that those neurons correspond cleanly to distinct concepts.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits essential SAE architecture and training details such as latent width, TopK value, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, epochs, auxiliary-loss settings, activation-sampling procedure, and compute. It also does not clearly specify train/validation/test splits or how per-concept multipliers were selected, leaving potential evaluation-set tuning unresolved. No code or artifact-release statement is provided.

The comparison protocol is difficult to audit because the authors state that they corrected an inconsistency in SAeUron's public metric implementation but do not identify the bug, give the corrected procedure precisely, or report how correction affects other baselines. Uncertainty is reported only for the main aggregate experiment, not the sequential, adversarial, or nudity results.

Presentation is polished overall, but important protocol differences are scattered: qualitative examples use only the last 25 steps and multiplier -1, whereas the main comparison uses all steps and searched per-object multipliers. Variant names are opaque, notation gamma is reused for decorrelation and intervention strength, and some causal explanations are asserted from correlations.

The work performs inference-time suppression through an attached SAE rather than removing information from the underlying diffusion-model weights. The original model remains intact and can generate the concept if the intervention is disabled or bypassed, so the paper should delimit its use of 'machine unlearning' and distinguish reversible filtering from data-deletion guarantees.

Limitations and ethics are not treated adequately. There is no dedicated limitations discussion of benchmark/classifier bias, NudeNet errors and demographic bias, adversarial bypass, reversibility, or the risks of treating imperfect suppression as regulatory deletion. The safety evaluation is relevant, but its detector-based conclusions require stronger qualification.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly motivated and proposes an intuitively useful supervised-SAE approach to inference-time concept suppression. The two-stage training method, losses, intervention rule, and main empirical claims are presented accessibly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/fd8e3f3bea744710805bb814c1a57f33/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reported UnlearnCanvas results are promising: the selected variant improves the mean of UA, IRA, and CRA from 82.29 to 91.51, reports four-seed variability, and obtains a lower FID than SAeUron. Sequential removal over nine object classes also suggests that supervised features may interfere less than the unsupervised baseline.

The evaluation is broader than a single headline table, covering multiplier sensitivity, sequential suppression, adversarial prompts, nudity detection, qualitative outputs, feature scores, and several loss variants.

Using prompt-derived labels is a practical way to supervise known concept dictionaries, and reducing intervention from many SAE latents to one or two could be operationally useful even if the result is better described as controllable suppression than machine unlearning.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central claim of an enforced one-to-one concept–latent mapping does not follow from the method. Φ independently assigns each concept its highest-scoring latent and is not constrained to be injective. The concept-assignment loss contains only a positive activation term and no concept-specific negative or exclusivity term. Moreover, the decorrelation loss separates object latents from style latents but does not separate different objects. Consistent with this, Table 8 reports 10 Cats–Dogs overlapping timesteps for the selected OS-DC-CA-FT model, equal to SAeUron, directly weakening the claimed prevention of feature splitting and interference.

The evidence for feature centralization is inadequate. The score plots cover only four hand-selected concepts, and a larger maximum score does not establish that all relevant information resides in one latent. The k-NN experiment is insufficiently specified—particularly how concept-dependent selected coordinates are combined, how train/test splits and feature selection are performed, and whether labels leak through the selection procedure—so Figure 5 cannot substantiate the strong sufficiency claim.

The work does not perform machine unlearning in the usual deletion sense: Stable Diffusion's weights and learned information remain intact, the intervention is reversible, and it can be disabled. It is an inference-time activation steering or content-suppression layer trained for a fixed, enumerated ontology. Sequential experiments concern concepts already included during SAE supervision and therefore do not demonstrate support for genuinely new deletion requests.

The comparison and tuning protocol is not sufficiently controlled. The paper states that it corrected an inconsistency in SAeUron's public metrics but never identifies the bug or provides the corrected procedure. It selects among numerous variants and per-object multipliers using a search, without specifying validation splits, selection criteria, or equivalent tuning budgets for baselines. Consequently, the reported 9.22-point gain may include model-selection advantages.

The 96.67% computational reduction counts only seven versus 210 inference evaluations and ignores supervised SAE fine-tuning, labeled activation generation, concept assignment, and variant selection. It is therefore a reduction in a narrowly defined multiplier/latent search, not overall computational cost. The choice of exactly 30 baseline latent combinations is also not justified.

Several auxiliary claims are overstated or internally inconsistent. Under UnlearnDiffAtk, SAEMNESIA still falls from 73.30% to 28.30% UA, and the unexplained pre-attack SAeUron value of 26.19% differs sharply from its 87.16% main-table UA. The claimed nudity state of the art requires two latents and a multiplier of -60, contradicting the single-latent narrative; the one-latent version is worse than SAeUron (47 versus 18 detections). No uncertainty is reported for these experiments.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance. There is no code or artifact statement, and key details are missing: optimizer, learning rate, epochs, batch size, SAE expansion dimension, TopK value, auxiliary-loss settings, activation sampling volume, evaluation sample counts, data splits, multiplier-selection protocol, hardware, and runtime. The statement that labels come at 'no additional cost' also overlooks the need to enumerate target concepts and construct supervised activation data.

Presentation is generally readable but makes repeated causal assertions unsupported by ablations, contains duplicated prose, calls FID a percentage, and provides dense qualitative grids that are difficult to assess. The paper lacks a dedicated limitations discussion. It briefly acknowledges failures on blended concepts and class imbalance but does not address reversibility, ontology dependence, classifier-based metric limitations, adversarial bypasses, or NudeNet's demographic and detection biases. These omissions are especially important for the safety framing. Overall, the idea and results have merit, but unsupported central claims and insufficient experimental specification prevent reliable acceptance.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses an important problem—targeted concept removal in diffusion models—and the inference-time SAE intervention is practically appealing because it avoids modifying the base model’s weights.

Empirical promise: On UnlearnCanvas, the reported headline result (94.65 UA, 91.39 IRA, and 88.48 CRA) substantially exceeds SAeUron and the other listed baselines. The proposed model also reports better FID than SAeUron (approximately 111 versus 124).

Breadth of evaluation: The experiments cover retention, generation quality, multiplier sensitivity, sequential removal, an adversarial attack, and I2P nudity suppression. Four-seed uncertainty is reported for the principal result, and the sequential experiment shows a large advantage after nine removals (92.4% versus 64% UA).

Originality: Supervised organization of diffusion-model SAE features for intervention is a useful extension of prior unsupervised SAE unlearning. Using prompt-derived labels makes the idea relatively simple to apply in controlled settings.

Presentation: The motivation, pipeline, and intervention are generally easy to follow. The score histograms, activation maps, qualitative grids, ablations, and explicit disclosure of difficult cases such as flames and jellyfish make the empirical behavior tangible.

Safety relevance: Testing adversarial prompting and NSFW suppression is valuable. The I2P result is promising: the two-latent variant yields 9 detections versus SAeUron’s 18 while retaining similar CLIPScore and FID.
weaknesses: Soundness—central claim: The stated one-to-one concept–latent mapping is not actually enforced by the objective. Each concept independently selects its highest-scoring latent, with no injective assignment constraint, while the concept-assignment loss contains only a positive term and does not penalize that latent on samples lacking the concept. L1 sparsity cannot by itself establish exclusivity. The reported model also has the same 10 Cats–Dogs overlapping timesteps as SAeUron in Table 8, directly weakening the claimed elimination of feature splitting.

Soundness—decorrelation loss: Equation 9 minimizes the signed Pearson correlation rather than its absolute value or square. As written, optimization rewards strong negative correlation instead of decorrelation. Moreover, it acts between broad object/style groups, not among concepts within the object group where the main one-to-one claim is needed.

Evidence for centralization is incomplete. Only four individual score distributions are shown, and a dominant peak does not demonstrate that the corresponding neuron is monosemantic or that no other concept shares it. The averaged k-NN result is insufficiently specified and lacks per-concept results, uncertainty, and a direct test of assignment uniqueness across all concepts.

The main quantitative result is internally inconsistent. Tables 1–2 report 94.65/91.39/88.48 with average 91.51, whereas Table 5 identifies the reported OS-DC-CA-FT model with 91.75/93.16/88.60; those latter values average to about 91.17, not the displayed 91.51. This undermines confidence in the headline comparison and must be reconciled.

Evaluation selection is unclear. Per-object multipliers are chosen through a search, but the manuscript does not clearly identify a disjoint validation set, raising possible test-set tuning concerns. The sequential experiment uses one selected nine-object subset and one order without uncertainty; adversarial robustness uses one attack and still falls sharply from 73.3% to 28.3%; and the claimed architecture agnosticism is not tested beyond closely related SD v1.x models.

The claim of 96.67% computational-cost reduction counts only 210 versus 7 inference evaluations. No wall-clock, memory, SAE-training cost, activation-collection cost, or comparison with end-to-end alternatives is reported. Describing supervision as coming at “no additional cost” is therefore too strong.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance in its current form. The paper does not provide a code or artifact link and omits important details such as SAE width, Top-K value, optimizer, learning rate, training duration, batch size, exact activation volume and splits, seed identities, and full procedures for multiplier selection and k-NN evaluation. Only several loss coefficients are supplied.

Limitations and ethics receive insufficient treatment. There is no dedicated limitations discussion addressing dependence on prompt-derived labels, ambiguous/compositional concepts, classifier-based evaluation, detector errors or demographic bias in NudeNet, and possible concept circumvention. The nudity result also requires two latents and a multiplier of −60, contradicting the general single-latent narrative and suggesting centralization is data-dependent.

strengths: Originality/significance: Supervised concept-aligned sparse autoencoders are a useful and reasonably novel direction for interpretable diffusion-model editing. Single-latent intervention, if validated, could materially simplify repeated concept erasure.

Empirical breadth: The paper evaluates object and style erasure, sequential requests, held-out concepts, adversarial prompts, nudity suppression, generation quality, and a preliminary second backbone. The gains over the closest SAE baseline are substantial on the main object benchmark: 91.51 versus 82.29 average.

The ablations compare fine-tuning versus training from scratch, alternative assignment losses, pre- versus post-TopK supervision, and uniform steering multipliers. Reporting four-seed uncertainty for the main method is also helpful.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and visually polished. The method is motivated intuitively, and the limitations section candidly discusses closed-vocabulary operation, within-group interference, architectural scope, and scaling to large vocabularies. Ethics: The impact statement appropriately recognizes both beneficial safety applications and risks from incomplete erasure, distribution shift, misuse, and false confidence; no unresolved ethical issue independently precludes publication.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that the method “enforces one-to-one concept-neuron mappings” is not supported by the objective. Each concept independently receives its highest-scoring latent, but no injectivity constraint prevents multiple concepts from receiving the same latent. The positive-only assignment loss encourages a designated latent to fire, but neither suppresses that latent for other concepts nor prevents other latents from encoding the target concept. Global L1 sparsity does not imply either property.

The paper contains direct evidence against the advertised mapping guarantee: for the reported OS-DC-CA-FT model, Table 11 shows Cats and Dogs sharing the most-active latent at 10 timesteps, equal to the unsupervised baseline. The decorrelation term only acts between macro-groups such as objects and styles, so it cannot resolve this within-object collision. Moreover, minimizing a raw Pearson correlation, rather than its magnitude or square, can reward negative correlation instead of decorrelation.

The feature-centralization validation is inadequate. A larger maximum score for a few selected concepts and similar k-NN accuracy from one latent do not demonstrate that information is absent from other latents; redundant distributed representations could yield the same observations. The paper needs an all-concept concentration metric, collision statistics, negative selectivity measurements, and intervention-based necessity/sufficiency tests on held-out data.

Evaluation validity is unclear because multiplier values are tuned separately by concept, yet the manuscript does not state which split or selection criterion determines them. The anchor prompts are explicitly reused for training and the “validation dataset,” and it is not established that benchmark test labels were excluded from multiplier or configuration selection. The reported 96.67% reduction counts seven versus 210 evaluations, not measured end-to-end computational cost, and omits the 27-configuration supervised-loss search and substantially higher SAE training cost.

Several headline conclusions are overstated. SAEmnesia is not the best object-erasure method in Table 1, and the claimed superiority is primarily over one SAE baseline. Sequential object evaluation uses nine selected concepts without uncertainty; held-out-style improvement is only 1.43 average points; and the preliminary SDXL-Turbo result has severe retention degradation (45.15 IRA) and lacks CRA. These results do not yet substantiate architecture-agnostic or broad scalability claims.

The nudity result conflicts with the core single-latent story: the default method is worse than SAeUron (47 versus 18 detections), while the highlighted result changes to two latents and an extreme multiplier of -600. This may still be practically interesting, but it should not be presented as confirmation of one-concept/one-neuron centralization.

Reproducibility is insufficient for reliable reconstruction. Missing or ambiguous details include the exact activation tensor and intervention hook, concept-assignment update schedule, number of training epochs, auxiliary-loss coefficient and dead-latent settings, delta in the score, evaluation sample counts and seeds for most experiments, multiplier-selection protocol, attack randomization, and complete prompt/data-generation details. The use of proprietary Claude-generated Ring-A-Bell pairs further complicates reproduction, and no code or artifact-release statement is provided.

Methodological notation is ambiguous: the score is timestep-dependent while the mapping is written as a single timestep-independent index; Equation 10 multiplies an activation by both gamma and its mean despite describing normalization, giving an unusual scale-dependent transformation; and its threshold alternates between statistics over D_c and D. These ambiguities affect the central intervention and must be resolved.

Presentation details also need correction: FID protocols and sample sizes are not specified, FID is incorrectly labeled as a percentage in places, reported FID values differ markedly across tables without sufficient explanation, and uncertainty or matched reruns are absent for most comparisons. Overall, the idea and empirical signal are promising, but the unsupported structural claim and evaluation ambiguities currently prevent others from relying on the conclusions.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper explores a useful direction—supervising SAE features to make diffusion-model interventions more localized—and the inference-time reversibility of attaching/detaching the SAE is practically attractive.

Empirical breadth: The evaluation covers object and style erasure, cumulative multi-concept intervention, adversarial prompts, nudity suppression, generation quality, and a preliminary second backbone. On UnlearnCanvas, the reported object metrics substantially improve over the closest SAE baseline (91.51 versus 82.29 average).

Presentation/ethics: The manuscript is generally readable and visually polished. It includes candid discussion of closed-vocabulary scaling, within-group interference, newer architectures, and possible misuse rather than concealing these limitations.
weaknesses: Soundness—central claim: The method does not actually enforce the advertised one-to-one concept–latent mapping. Φ(c)=argmax_i score(i,c) need not be injective, and the positive-only assignment loss merely raises a designated latent for positive examples; it neither suppresses that latent for other concepts nor prevents several concepts from choosing the same latent. Indeed, Table 11 reports Cats and Dogs sharing the top latent at all 10 timesteps for the main OS-DC-CA-FT model. Thus the central claims of eliminating feature splitting, monosemanticity, and one-to-one binding are unsupported and partly contradicted by the results.

Soundness: The proposed “decorrelation” objective minimizes the signed Pearson correlation itself, rather than its absolute value or square. Negative correlation therefore lowers the loss and is actively preferred, so Equation (9) does not mathematically enforce decorrelation. It also operates only between macro-groups, leaving object–object and style–style interference untreated, and the handling of zero-variance activations is unspecified.

Evidence for feature centralization is inadequate and potentially circular. Figure 4 and Appendix A.6 show only four selected score histograms out of 70 concepts, with no aggregate concentration, uniqueness, or collision statistic. The k-NN experiment is insufficiently specified: Figure 5 has a 5% random baseline suggestive of 20-way classification, yet “top-1 single feature” appears to use a different label-selected feature for each object, which could leak the target identity. Train/validation/test separation for feature selection and k-NN fitting is not stated.

The claimed 96.67% computational reduction is a reduction in one hand-defined multiplier/feature-combination search, not demonstrated end-to-end compute. It excludes the method’s 27-configuration training grid and roughly 5.4× per-step SAE training cost reported in Table 3. The baseline’s fixed 7×30 search space is asserted rather than justified, while SAEmnesia still uses separately tuned object multipliers in Table 6. Calling this a 96.67% computational-cost reduction is therefore misleading.

Evaluation and tuning protocols are under-specified. The manuscript says anchor prompts are also used as validation data; it does not clearly state how multiplier values and model variants are selected without test-set feedback. Sample counts, reference distributions, and uncertainty are missing for FID and most attack/sequential results. FID also changes from 111.16 for the main model in Table 8 to 56.15 in Table 15 without an adequate explanation of the aggregation or protocol.

Several headline extensions weaken rather than validate the main thesis. Standard one-latent SAEmnesia performs worse than SAeUron on nudity (47 versus 18 detections); the claimed state of the art requires two latents and an extreme multiplier of -600, contradicting the single-latent premise. The SDXL-Turbo experiment has only 54.39 average with IRA falling to 45.15 and lacks CRA, so it is preliminary rather than evidence of architecture-agnosticism. “Sequential unlearning” is only cumulative inference-time steering of nine selected objects, not a general sequential-update study.

Reproducibility is not adequate. Missing details include training duration and schedule, exact activation/sample construction, assignment update procedure, δ, auxiliary-loss settings, SAE dimensions, multiplier-selection criterion, evaluation sample counts, seeds for most experiments, and generated Ring-A-Bell prompts. No code or artifact commitment is provided. These omissions prevent reliable reconstruction of the central results.

Presentation/originality: The supervised positive activation loss and cross-group correlation penalty are relatively incremental additions to the cited SAE baseline, while the paper repeatedly overstates what they establish. The equation-level deficiencies and lack of direct validation of injective mappings are material, not merely presentational. The limitations section is welcome but does not acknowledge these decisive failures of the central formulation.

strengths: Soundness/evidence: The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for an SAE-based concept-erasure paper. On UnlearnCanvas object removal, SAEmnesia improves over the directly comparable SAeUron baseline across UA, IRA, and CRA, raising their average from 82.29% to 91.51%. It also reports four-seed variability, multiplier sweeps, FID, qualitative results, adversarial attacks, sequential erasure, held-out styles, and nudity suppression.

Significance: Concentrating a concept intervention into one or very few SAE latents is practically useful. The nine-object sequential experiment is particularly compelling: SAEmnesia retains 92.4% UA versus 64% for SAeUron while also improving retention accuracy. The method is reversible and adds little inference overhead.

Originality: Supervised concept-latent assignment is a natural but meaningful extension of unsupervised SAE-based erasure. Using prompt-derived labels, a concept-assignment loss, and cross-group decorrelation to reduce feature splitting offers a clear mechanistic contribution rather than merely another weight-fine-tuning objective.

Presentation: The motivation, pipeline, evaluation metrics, and connection between feature centralization and efficient intervention are explained clearly. The appendix includes useful implementation hyperparameters, variants, compute measurements, per-concept multipliers, and limitations.

Ethics/limitations: The paper appropriately discusses misuse, incomplete erasure, distribution shift, closed-vocabulary behavior, similar-concept interference, and scaling beyond 70 concepts. The safety experiments are relevant, and the limitations discussion is candid rather than perfunctory.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of an enforced one-to-one mapping is stronger than the formulation supports. Φ is defined as a function from concepts to latent indices but is not constrained to be injective, so multiple concepts may select the same latent. Moreover, the concept-assignment loss rewards a designated latent only when its concept is present; it contains no explicit negative or exclusivity term suppressing that latent for other concepts. L1 sparsity does not by itself establish one-to-one correspondence.

The decorrelation objective minimizes the raw Pearson correlation rather than its absolute value or square. Consequently, it rewards strong negative correlation, not statistical decorrelation. This weakens the stated interpretation of Equation (9) and warrants either correction or evidence that negative-correlation solutions do not arise.

Evidence for feature centralization is incomplete. Only a handful of score histograms are shown, while the averaged k-NN experiment is insufficiently specified and lacks uncertainty. More importantly, Table 11 reports that the selected fine-tuned SAEmnesia configuration has the same 10 Cats-Dogs overlapping timesteps as SAeUron, despite reduced concept interference being a central motivation. A full collision matrix, per-concept centralization statistics, and comparisons against matched supervised controls are needed.

Reproducibility/reporting: Important training details remain missing, including training duration or stopping rule, exact activation-dataset size and sampling, assignment-update procedure, evaluation sample counts, and the split used to select per-concept multipliers. There is also an apparent inconsistency between Table 1 and Table 8 for the same OS-DC-CA-FT model: Table 1 reports 94.65/91.39/88.48, whereas Table 8 reports 91.75/93.16/88.60 while retaining the same 91.51 average. No code or checkpoint release commitment is stated.

The advertised 96.67% computational reduction concerns only a hand-specified inference hyperparameter search, not total cost. The appendix shows SAEmnesia training batches take about 385 ms versus 71 ms for SAeUron and additionally uses a 27-configuration loss grid. The paper should distinguish search-space reduction from end-to-end computational savings and report total GPU-hours.

Scope/significance: This is reversible inference-time concept suppression rather than deletion of training-data influence or irreversible model unlearning; detaching the SAE restores the concept exactly. Results are concentrated on SD v1.x and a benchmark with templated prompts and fixed classifiers. The SDXL-Turbo result has only 54.39 average accuracy with substantial retention loss, so the architecture-agnostic and broader unlearning claims remain preliminary.

The nudity result qualifies the single-latent thesis: the nominal one-latent SAEmnesia model is worse than SAeUron (47 versus 18 detections), and the reported best result requires two latents and an extreme multiplier of -600. This is still useful, but it should be framed as evidence that feature centralization can fail under imbalanced or broad concepts rather than as straightforward validation of one-neuron erasure.
